opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the reasoning comes down to a few things, and some are about the world and some are about NVIDIA specifically.

First, look at where AI has made the most progress so far. Large language models have been incredible, but they mostly live in the digital world: text, code, images. Yet most of the global economy is physical. Manufacturing, logistics, transportation, agriculture, healthcare. Factories, warehouses, cars, robots. If AI is going to have its biggest impact, it eventually has to understand and act in the physical world. That's a huge opportunity, and it's still largely untapped.

Second, physical AI is a very hard problem, and hard problems need a lot of compute. You need models that understand physics, space, cause and effect, how objects move and interact. Training those models takes enormous amounts of data, and real-world data is expensive, slow, and sometimes dangerous to collect. You can't crash a thousand cars to teach a self-driving system. So you need simulation, synthetic data, and world models that can generate realistic futures. All of that is extremely compute-intensive. That's naturally where NVIDIA can contribute.

Third, NVIDIA has been building toward this for a long time, even before people called it "physical AI." We have deep roots in graphics, which is really about simulating light and physics. We have Omniverse for simulation and digital twins, Isaac for robotics, and the DRIVE platform for autonomous vehicles. And on the research side, many of us have worked for years on generative models and video synthesis. When you put graphics, simulation, generative AI, and accelerated computing together, physical AI is almost the natural intersection.

And finally, I'd say the way NVIDIA thinks about it is as a full-stack problem. Robotics companies need what we sometimes call three computers: one to train the models in the data center, one to simulate and test them, and one that runs on the robot itself. NVIDIA can provide all three. So rather than building every robot ourselves, we want to be the platform that enables the whole ecosystem, with world foundation models like Cosmos, simulation tools, and the hardware underneath, so that developers everywhere can build physical AI faster.

So for me it felt like the right timing, the right problem, and the right company to tackle it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that physical AI is where the atoms are. If you look at the world economy, the vast majority of it is physical. Manufacturing, logistics, transportation, agriculture, construction, healthcare. These are industries worth tens of trillions of dollars, and almost none of that value has been touched by AI yet. Language models changed how we work with information, but information work is actually a small slice of what humans do. Most of what the economy does is move things, build things, inspect things, and that all happens in the physical world.

So when we asked ourselves where the next big wave would be, the answer was clear. The question was really whether we were ready for it, and whether the technology was ready.

And this is where it connects naturally to what NVIDIA has always been. People sometimes forget that we started as a company that simulates physics. Graphics is physics, it is light transport, it is materials, it is how objects interact. We spent decades building simulation, ray tracing, physics engines, and then on top of that we built the accelerated computing stack that trained all the foundation models. Physical AI sits exactly at the intersection of those two things. You need simulation to generate the data, because you cannot crash a million cars or break a million robots in the real world. And you need large-scale model training to learn from that data. We already had both halves.

There is also a data problem that makes physical AI very different from language. For LLMs, the internet gave everyone the training set for free. There is no internet of robot experience. Every robot action, every sensor reading, every interaction with the environment has to be collected or synthesized. That is a hard problem, and hard problems are where we tend to do well, because the solution requires full-stack thinking. Simulation, world models, data pipelines, the robot computer on the edge, the training infrastructure in the data center. No single piece solves it.

And honestly, part of it is timing. A few years ago the models simply were not good enough to understand the world. With the progress in generative models, we now have systems that can predict what happens next in a video, that understand physics implicitly, that can reason about space and time. That capability unlocks everything. Once a model can imagine what the world will look like after an action, you can use it to train robots, to test autonomous vehicles, to plan. That is what we are building with world foundation models. So it was not that we chose physical AI arbitrarily. The capability arrived, the market was enormous and untouched, and it happened to require exactly the set of things we had been building for thirty years.

r002.rationale: It describes NVIDIA’s simulation, model training, and computing stack, but does not distinguish helping developers build products from operating consumer-facing applications.

astra-6.text:
I think physical AI is a natural next step: taking AI beyond processing information and enabling it to act in the physical world. But that introduces a different set of challenges. A robot needs to understand its surroundings, reason about what might happen next, and choose an action that works under real physical constraints.

That makes it a good fit for NVIDIA because the challenge spans computing, simulation, and learning. You need compute to train the models, simulation to develop and test them, and computing on the machine itself to make decisions in real time. Those pieces need to work together.

And the opportunity extends across many kinds of machines. If you can build a foundation that helps developers teach machines to perceive and act, that can support applications in manufacturing, transportation, and other parts of the physical economy.

r001.rationale: The response describes physical AI and applications across industries, but does not mention population aging as a source of demand.

r002.rationale: It says NVIDIA can support developers, but does not distinguish that role from operating consumer-facing applications itself.

sol-6.1.text:
When I think about physical AI, I think about bringing intelligence into systems that need to understand and act in the real world—robots, autonomous vehicles, and industrial machines. That requires more than recognizing what’s in an image. You have to understand how the world changes and what will happen when you take an action.

That makes it a natural fit for NVIDIA, because the challenge spans computing, AI training, simulation, and deployment. You need to train models, give them environments where they can learn and be tested, and then run them efficiently in a physical system.

The opportunity is to connect those pieces. If we can make that development cycle faster and more accessible, we can help people build useful machines across many different industries.
